lessons.title: Stories Across Mediums
lessons.originalProblem: Thin on the actual standard — RL.4.7 is about how a visual/oral presentation reflects specific text descriptions, but the lesson stays at a generic 'movies cut and add scenes' level and never models connecting a specific text moment to its visual realization.

steps.ttsScript: A story can be read as words, or watched as a movie.
Today we line up a story's exact words with what we see on screen.
Authors give us exact details, like a green cloak with a silver clasp.
steps.displayText: Story details: green cloak, silver clasp

steps.ttsScript: A good movie shows those very things on screen, not just any cloak.
Let's try one. Here is a line from a story.
The old lighthouse glowed red as waves crashed against the rocks.
steps.displayText: Lighthouse glowed red, waves crashed on rocks.

steps.ttsScript: Which thing must the movie show? A red glowing light!
And one more? Waves crashing on the rocks!
Here is a handy trick to remember.
Point to the exact words, then find that very thing on screen.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, director! Here is a sentence: A small fox darted past the frozen pond as snow fell in big white flakes. To match these exact words, what must the movie show on screen?

choices: A fox by a frozen pond, snow falling
A bright sunny meadow in spring
How lonely the fox is feeling
interactive.correct: A fox by a frozen pond, snow falling
interactive.correctScript: Yes! A fox by a frozen pond with snow falling. You matched the exact words to the screen!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Look back at the words a camera could really show. A fox, a frozen pond, falling snow. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's line up more story words with the screen.

slides.prompt: A student reads a chapter about a thunderstorm, then watches a movie version with dramatic music and dark lighting. The movie version adds —
choices: Mood and atmosphere through sound and visuals
slides.correct: Mood and atmosphere through sound and visuals

slides.prompt: When a book is turned into a play, what might be LOST?
choices: The character's inner thoughts described by the narrator
slides.correct: The character's inner thoughts described by the narrator

slides.prompt: What might a visual presentation (movie or play) ADD to a story that the text cannot?
choices: Facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language of actors
slides.correct: Facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language of actors

slides.prompt: A book describes a character as "a tall woman with kind eyes." In the movie, the actress has a warm smile and speaks softly. How does the movie expand on the text?
choices: It shows specific visual and audio details that bring 'kind eyes' to life
slides.correct: It shows specific visual and audio details that bring 'kind eyes' to life

slides.prompt: Imagine reading a book where a wizard's tower is described as being made of smooth, black stone, reaching high into the clouds, with a giant, glowing crystal at the very top. If the movie adaptation of this story shows the wizard's tower as a short, brick building with a regular antenna, what is the biggest difference a reader would notice between the book and the movie?
choices: The movie version has more exciting characters.
The overall message of the story is changed in the movie.
How the wizard's tower appears is very different in each version.
The movie tells the story much faster than the book.
slides.correct: How the wizard's tower appears is very different in each version.

lessons.title: Reading Big Stories
lessons.originalProblem: It teaches reading-stamina study skills, not comprehension of complex text — it sidesteps what the standard is actually about

steps.ttsScript: When a story gets longer, we read closely to understand it.
We watch the characters, the problem, and the small details.
Good readers ask who the story is about.
Then they ask what that person wants.
Watch for little signs
that show a hero's mood
and what they do next.
Let's try one together. Here's part of a longer story.
Maya stared at the dark cave. Her hands shook, but she wanted to find her lost dog.
steps.displayText: Maya stared at the dark cave. Her hands shook, but she wanted to find her lost dog.

steps.ttsScript: How does Maya feel? Scared. Her shaking hands are the sign.
What does Maya want? To find her dog. That is why she keeps going.
Scared, but brave! You read the signs and understood Maya.
Here is a helpful trick.
Make a movie in your mind as you read each scene!
steps.displayText: Make a movie in your mind

steps.ttsScript: Then the little signs become easy to spot!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Here's a new story. The judge read Lena's name, and the whole crowd cheered. She held up her science ribbon and couldn't stop grinning. What is Lena most likely feeling at the science fair?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Proud! Holding up her ribbon and grinning after winning was the sign!
interactive.wrongScript: Almost! She won a ribbon, held it up high, and couldn't stop grinning. How would that make her feel? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Now you'll read story bits on your own.
Follow each character and read the little signs.

slides.prompt:
Nobody knew where the music came from. Every night at midnight, a violin played from somewhere deep in the woods. The townspeople locked their doors and whispered about ghosts. Only young Alma grabbed her lantern and followed the sound.

What does Alma's action reveal about her?
choices: She's curious and braver than the other townspeople
slides.correct: She's curious and braver than the other townspeople

slides.prompt:
The treaty was signed on a Tuesday. By Wednesday, the two kingdoms had already broken it. **Peace,** the old queen muttered, "is harder to keep than to promise."

What is the queen's message about peace?
choices: Making peace is simple but maintaining it is the real challenge
slides.correct: Making peace is simple but maintaining it is the real challenge

slides.prompt:
Theo didn't notice the first leaf fall. Or the second. But by the time the maple tree was half bare, he understood what his grandmother meant when she said, "Change happens slowly, then all at once."

What is Grandmother's saying about?
choices: How change in life can be gradual then suddenly obvious
slides.correct: How change in life can be gradual then suddenly obvious

slides.prompt:
Zuri had two rules: never break a promise, and always carry a pencil. **You never know,** she said, "when you'll need to write something down before you forget it — or before someone tries to make you forget."

What does the second rule suggest about Zuri?
choices: She values truth and recording important things
slides.correct: She values truth and recording important things

slides.prompt:
The ship had been at sea for thirty-seven days. Fresh water was running low, and the crew whispered about turning back. Captain Adaeze stood at the bow, eyes fixed on the horizon. **Land by sunrise,** she said. Nobody believed her. But at dawn, there it was.

What theme does this passage suggest?
choices: Faith and determination can lead you through doubt
slides.correct: Faith and determination can lead you through doubt

lessons.title: Parts of a Book
lessons.originalProblem: Only 1 practice MCQ (vs. 5 in the siblings), so the kid gets almost no independent reps after instruction; the lesson also slightly overstuffs the teach slide with four parts at once before any practice.

steps.ttsScript: Did you know a book has special parts, just like your body does?
Today we'll meet the front cover, the back cover, and the title page.
Let's see what each one does!
The front cover is the very first thing you see. It shows the title and a picture.

displayParts.text: Front cover: first thing you see

steps.ttsScript: Flip the book over to the other side. That's the back cover.
Open the book and look inside. The first page is the title page.
The title page names the book and tells who made it.
Let's try one together! Here is a brand-new book.
On the front you see a big spider and the words All About Bugs.
What part shows the picture and the name? The front cover!
Where do we find who made it? The title page inside!
You spotted both parts. You're a book expert!
Here's a trick. The cover is on the outside, and the title page is on the inside.
Outside greets you, inside tells who made it!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try, detective! Sam opened his book all the way to the inside. The first page named the book and showed who wrote it. What part did Sam find?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! The title page! It's inside and tells who made the book. You found it all by yourself!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Sam was looking inside the book at who made it. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Great work learning the parts of a book!
Your turn now. Let's spot some book parts!

slides.prompt:
Captain Ava picked up her ocean book. She turned it over to read what the book is about.

Which PART of the book did Captain Ava look at?

The explorer opened the book and saw the name of the book and who wrote it on the very first page inside.

What is that PAGE called?

The explorer wanted to know who wrote the book about dolphins. She opened the book and looked at the first page inside.

Where did she find the AUTHOR's name?
